finding: The live range of $180-$925 is about right for one engine mount on a mainstream vehicle: the bottom sits at or slightly above the cheapest totals that can be built, and the top covers everything built here but not what the benchmarks show for a larger luxury car. Built totals for ONE mount, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Honda Civic Si side mount about $155-$854 (0.6-0.7 hr; an $83 aftermarket mount to Honda's $742 list price for this fluid-filled mount); midsize 2017 Mazda CX-5 right-side mount about $131-$261 (0.5-0.6 hr; $71 aftermarket to $165 Mazda list); luxury 2015 Acura ILX 2.4L side mount about $179-$701 (0.8-2.0 hr; the same $83 aftermarket mount to Acura's $381 list price). Truck 2016 Silverado 1500 5.3L: the part is $48 (aftermarket) to $220 (GM list) per mount, but GM states a time only for both mounts (3.2 hr), so the low hours figure is still null and there is no low total; the most one mount could come to at that both-sides time is about $732 ($220 + 3.2 hr x $160), a ceiling and not an estimate. About the luxury total: the 0.8 hr is Acura's own time for this ILX mount, so about $179-$509 is what the ILX job itself builds to; the 2.0 hr top is Acura's time to diagnose and replace the active rear mount on a 2018-2019 MDX, a larger vehicle and a dearer part that was not priced, so $701 is a rough upper bound and understates an active-mount job. The luxury example was switched from the 2015 Cadillac ATS 3.6L because no aftermarket mount for it turned up in the catalogs loaded or in two further searches and GM prints a time only for both mounts (1.1 hr); for the record the ATS mount is $179 at GM list ($243 all-wheel drive), about $103 at the cheapest genuine price seen, and one mount could not exceed about $355 at the both-mounts time. The ILX is a compact car built on the Civic's platform, so this class sits low for luxury cars in general. The bottom: $131-$179 pairs an online aftermarket price with a manufacturer warranty time, the low end of what shops bill, so $180 is a fair floor for a simple mount. The top: $925 covers the dearest total built here ($854, the Civic Si with a dealer-list mount) and RepairPal's national $643-$798, but RepairPal puts a 2015 ATS at $952-$1,248 and YourMechanic averages $1,011 for a Civic, and Jerry gives $500-$1,500 for hydraulic or active mounts and hard-to-reach jobs. Why the benchmarks sit well above our built totals: they assume far more labor. RepairPal's $328-$481 of labor is roughly 2-4 hours at $120-$160/hr and Jerry says a shop typically takes 1.5-4.0 hours, against warranty times of 0.5-0.8 hr for one easy-to-reach mount; they may also cover more than one mount (none of them says). So expect real quotes for one mount to land in the upper half of the live range more often than our low totals suggest, and above it for larger luxury cars, active mounts or a full set. How solid the parts prices are: the Honda bulletin names part 50820-TR7-305, which no catalog loaded lists; the price used is for 50820-TR7-A01, the only side mount Honda's catalog lists for the 2012-2015 Si, and the two are not confirmed to be the same part. The Acura list price is for 50820-TX6-A01, the number the Acura bulletin names for the 2.4L, but a retailer's catalog instead lists the Civic Si part 50820-TR7-A01 (list $742) for the ILX 2.4L; if that is the right part the ILX top would be about $1,062, above the live range. The Mazda list price is for K156-39-060, the right-side mount of the 2.5L engine sold in the United States, not the bulletin's K1Y0-39-060 (2.0L, Canada and Mexico); the aftermarket CX-5 price comes from a listing that names the 2017 CX-5 but not the engine. The GM number priced for the Silverado (84175580) is the current catalog number. How solid the labor times are: economy's high and luxury's low are for the example vehicles and for one mount (Honda 0.7 hr, Acura 0.8 hr). Economy's low is a Mazda3. Midsize is the right model but an engine not sold in the United States, plus a Jeep Compass rear mount. Luxury's high is a different vehicle and a different, active mount, with diagnosis included. Truck is for the example vehicle but for BOTH mounts: GM has one-side operations ('Engine Mount Replacement - Left Side' and '- Right Side') but every bulletin found says only 'use published time', and searches for a stated one-mount time on any other full-size pickup (Ram, Ford, Nissan, Toyota) found none, so the low end stays null and the high end is a ceiling at warranty pace. All are warranty times. Body-on-frame trucks and SUVs take much longer than small cars: GM allows 3.1-3.2 hr for both mounts on a 2014-2018 Silverado/Sierra and 3.8 hr on the SUVs, and 13.4 hr for 'Engine Mount Replacement' on the 2019-2021 Silverado/Sierra 5.3L and 6.2L; FCA allows 3.9 hr for both on a 2021-2022 Jeep Grand Cherokee 3.6L, 2.0 hr for both on a 2015 Grand Cherokee diesel and 1.4 hr for both on a Ram 2500 6.4L; a transmission mount on a 2019-2020 Silverado is 0.5 hr. The only active-mount times found are Acura's 2.0 hr for the MDX rear mount and Porsche's 685-761 time units for both mounts on a 2020 911, not converted to hours. Still missing: a stated one-mount time for the truck class, a price for an active mount, and a J.D. Power figure (its page would not load). An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or inspection fee (finding which mount has failed), new one-time-use mount bolts and nuts (the Honda bulletin calls for four new bolts and a nut with one mount), and a second or third mount, since they tend to wear together and some makers replace them only in pairs. Active, hydraulic (fluid-filled) and electronically controlled mounts cost far more than plain rubber ones and may need a separate actuator or vacuum line. On some vehicles the job needs an engine support, removal of the splash shields or exhaust parts, or a wheel alignment if the subframe is loosened. Also shop supplies and sales tax.
